name: Ḥammād ibn Abī Laylā Maysara (or Sābūr), known as Ḥammād al-Rāwiya
summary: Kufan 'transmitter' of the old poetry and the reports of the Arabs, favourite of the Umayyad caliph Yazīd II, whom al-Naḥḥās names as the collector of the Seven Long Poems (al-Muʿallaqāt).
bio: Ḥammād of Kufa was famous for transmitting poems and reports; Ibn al-Anbārī cites al-Naḥḥās that it was he who gathered the Seven Long Poems, and adds that the story of their being hung on the Kaʿba is not established.

Most of his entry is his own tale of the Umayyad court: attached to Yazīd ibn ʿAbd al-Malik and therefore cold-shouldered by his brother Hishām, he was later summoned by Hishām to Damascus to recite a forgotten poem, and sent home rewarded. Al-Zubaydī opens his list of the lexicographers of Kufa with a 'Ḥammād ibn Hurmuz, Abū Laylā'.
uncertain: That al-Zubaydī's 'Ḥammād ibn Hurmuz, called Abū Laylā' is Ḥammād al-Rāwiya rests on the kunya: the sources call his father Abū Laylā Maysara, or Sābūr.
The year of his death is not in Ibn al-Anbārī; the later sources give about 155/772 (some 156 or 158).

sources.title: Ibn al-Anbārī, Nuzhat al-alibbāʾ fī ṭabaqāt al-udabāʾ (Cairo 1294/1877), pp. 43–50
